## SEO Site Audit: A Small Business Owner’s Step-by-Step Guide


Your website looks professional. Your services are clearly listed. So why does a competitor with a less polished site keep showing up above you in search?


An SEO (search engine optimization) site audit can help you find the answer. Problems such as a service page Google can’t index, slow load times, weak content, or inconsistent local business information can make it harder for customers to find you. More customers now use[AI search](https://www.thryv.com/blog/what-is-ai-search/) like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini to find local businesses. Showing up in those answers is called[answer engine optimization (AEO)](https://www.thryv.com/blog/answer-engine-optimization-business-visibility-ai-search/) , and this guide shows you how to check for your business.


Free audit tools can flag potential problems, but a score or list of warnings won’t tell you what deserves attention first. This guide walks you through a practical first-pass audit so you can identify and prioritize the fixes most likely to improve your visibility and help turn searches into calls, bookings, and inquiries.

## **What Is an SEO Site Audit (and Why Does It Matter for a Local Business)?**


An SEO site audit reviews your website and online presence for issues that may make it harder for customers to find your business in search. The goal is to identify what could be hurting your visibility and decide what deserves attention first.


Here is why it matters to you: In a[2026 Small Business Expo survey](https://www.thesmallbusinessexpo.com/blog/most-smbs-lack-seo-strategy/) , 55.6% of small businesses said they don’t invest in SEO at all. Nearly 60% describe their search visibility as poor or average. If your competitors don’t audit their sites, that’s a great opportunity for you.


A useful audit looks at five parts of[SEO for small businesses](https://www.thryv.com/blog/seo-for-small-businesses/) :


- **Technical SEO:** Can search engines find, load, and index your important pages?
- **On-page SEO:** Do those pages clearly explain your services and what searches they’re relevant to?
- **Content:** Does your website answer potential customers’ questions?
- **Site structure:** Can customers and search engines easily reach your important pages?
- **Local and off-site signals:** Is your business information accurate across your website, Google Business Profile, and other places customers search?


Use what you find to build your action plan. A service page that isn’t appearing in Google deserves more attention than a minor issue on an old blog post that rarely gets traffic.

## **How to Do an SEO Site Audit, Step by Step**


Start with your homepage and the service and location pages connected to the work you want more of. Work through these five areas to identify problems before deciding what to fix first. Keep a log with notes about the problem, the affected page, why it matters, who will fix it, and when.


### 1. Check Technical SEO: Can Search Engines Find and Load Your Site?


Start with the basics: Can Google access your important pages, and can customers use them without problems? This technical audit can uncover issues that hurt organic search visibility or user experience.


Check for:


- **Indexing:** Use Google Search Console’s[URL Inspection tool](https://www.seo-stack.io/blog/the-complete-guide-to-google-search-consoles-url-inspection-tool) to see whether an important page is indexed (stored in Google’s index) and eligible to appear in Google Search. A site:yourwebsite.com search can provide a quick spot check, but doesn’t show everything that’s indexed.
- **Blocked pages:** Look for important pages accidentally marked “[noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) ” or otherwise blocked from search engines.
- **Broken pages and links:** Fix links that lead to[404 errors](https://www.networksolutions.com/blog/what-is-a-404-error/) , especially along the path to a service, contact, or booking page.
- **Security:** Your website should use[HTTPS](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/ssl/what-is-https/) . To test it, open your site in a browser and look for a padlock icon next to the web address. If you see a “Not secure” warning instead, it’s time to switch to HTTPS.
- **Mobile usability:** Open your site on your phone. Make sure you can read the text, use the menu, tap the phone number, and complete a form easily.
- **Page speed:** Test important pages with[Google’s PageSpeed Insights](https://pagespeed.web.dev/) . Focus on major performance problems that make pages noticeably slow or difficult to use.
- **Redirects and duplicate pages:** Look for old URLs that lead to the wrong place or multiple URLs showing substantially the same page.
- **Sitemap:** Check that your[XML sitemap](https://searchengineland.com/tools/xml-sitemap-generator) includes the pages you want search engines to find and has been submitted through Google Search Console.
- Structured data: Apply[LocalBusiness schema](https://www.thryv.com/blog/schema-markup-for-small-businesses-aeo-guide/) . It’s code that describes your business in a format that Google and AI search engines read directly.


Prioritize anything preventing a key page from being found or used. If your air-conditioning repair page isn’t indexed in the middle of summer, that deserves attention before a minor speed recommendation on an old blog post.

### 2. Check On-Page SEO: Does Each Important Page Clearly Explain What You Offer?


Review your homepage and the service and location pages most likely to generate business.


For each page, ask:


- Does the **page title** clearly describe the primary service or topic?
- Is there one clear **main heading (H1)** ?
- Does the copy specifically explain the service?
- If location matters, does the page establish where you provide it?
- Does the **meta description** accurately summarize the page?
- Do important images have useful alt text?
- Is there a clear next step, such as calling, requesting a quote, or booking?
- Do multiple pages cover essentially the same service?


A simple test is whether someone can quickly tell what you offer, where you offer it, and what to do next.


If a general “Services” page briefly mentions drain cleaning, water heater repair, sewer repair, and emergency plumbing, for example, important services may deserve dedicated pages. Our[guide to SEO for plumbers](https://www.thryv.com/blog/seo-for-plumbers/) shows how to structure those pages. Keyword research can help you understand how customers search for those services and what language to use.


### 3. Audit Your Content: Are You Answering the Questions Customers Actually Search?


Content audits help you decide what to improve, update, combine, or create. Start by listing the jobs you most want customers to find you for, then check whether your website provides enough useful information about each one.


Look for:


- **Missing service pages:** Important services that have little or no dedicated information.
- **Thin pages:** Pages that don’t give customers enough information to understand the service or decide what to do next.
- **Outdated information:** Old hours, service areas, prices, offers, staff information, or services.
- **Duplicate content:** Pages that substantially repeat one another without serving a distinct purpose.
- **Unanswered customer questions:** Questions you regularly hear on calls, in emails, or during estimates.
- **Existing pages with potential:** Use Google Search Console to find pages appearing in search but receiving relatively few clicks. If you use Google Analytics, review which pages receive organic traffic and what visitors do after they arrive.


For SEO and AI-powered discovery, make sure important pages clearly state the service, relevant details, and location, and directly answer common customer questions.


Prioritize content tied to services customers can hire you for. Improving a weak high-value service page may deserve attention before publishing another general blog post.


### 4. Check Site Structure: Can Customers and Search Engines Reach Your Important Pages?


Starting from your homepage, see how easily a new visitor can reach your important services.


Check:


- **Navigation:** Are your core services easy to find?
- **Buried pages:** Do high-priority services have a clear path from your homepage or main service navigation?
- **Orphan pages:** Does every important page have at least one link pointing to it from another page on your site? A page without an inbound link is called an orphan page. Search engines may miss it during their crawling process.
- **Internal links:** Do related pages connect naturally? For example, a water-heater maintenance article could link to your repair or installation service.
- **Service and location organization:** Are related service and location pages organized clearly?
- **Mobile navigation and contact paths:** Can mobile visitors easily find services, call, request information, or book the next step?


Focus on pages tied to important services and new business opportunities.


### 5. Check Local and Off-Site SEO Signals: Does Your Business Look Consistent and Trustworthy Across the Web?


Your business details should match everywhere customers may find you. For a local business, your[Google Business Profile](https://www.thryv.com/reference/google-business-profile/) and other online directories can affect whether you appear in Google Maps and other local search results.


Compare your website with your major profiles and[business listings](https://www.thryv.com/reference/listings-management/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=OrganicSocial) . Check:


- Business name, address, and phone number
- Website URL
- Business hours
- Services and categories
- Service areas
- Recent customer reviews
- Outdated or duplicate listings


Prioritize inconsistencies that could cost you a customer. If your website lists Saturday hours but Google says you’re closed, someone looking for weekend service may call another business.


Also check whether you’re receiving recent reviews and responding to customers. Then look for relevant sites that mention or link to your business, such as local Chamber of Commerce sites, professional associations, supplier directories, community organizations, and local publications.


[Local Listings Management](https://www.thryv.com/features/local-listings/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=OrganicSocial) helps businesses manage accurate information across online directories from one place, while[Reputation Management](https://www.thryv.com/features/reputation-management/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=OrganicSocial) helps owners monitor and respond to customer reviews.


After you complete these five checks, prioritize your findings before making changes.


## **How to Prioritize What Your SEO Site Audit Finds**


For every issue you find, answer four questions:


- **What’s wrong?** Describe the specific problem.
- **Which pages does it affect?** Give priority to important service and location pages.
- **Why does it matter?** Could it affect visibility, user experience, or a customer’s ability to contact you?
- **What happens next?** Identify the fix, who can handle it, and when it needs attention.


Then work through your findings in this order:


**Impact vs. Effort** **Lower effort** **Higher effort**


Higher impact Do first: Remove an accidental noindex tag, fix broken links to key pages, improve missing titles or H1s Schedule next: Improve site speed, rebuild thin service pages, restructure confusing navigation


Lower impact Batch together: Clean up secondary metadata, add useful internal links, update older supporting pages Leave for later: Major changes with little expected effect on visibility or customer experience


Choose a few high-impact fixes to tackle first, then put the rest into a backlog you can work through over time. ## **DIY or Hand It Off? Deciding What to Do Yourself**


You can audit your own website and handle many SEO fixes yourself. The decision to bring in help usually comes down to the complexity of the work and how much time you want to spend maintaining your SEO.


### What SEO Audit Fixes Can You Handle Yourself?


Straightforward DIY fixes include:


- Rewriting vague page titles and headings
- Improving thin service pages
- Updating hours, services, locations, or contact information
- Adding internal links
- Fixing straightforward broken links
- Correcting your Google Business Profile and other listings
- Answering common customer questions


Start with high-impact, lower-effort fixes. Keep a record of what you change and when so you can track visibility, organic traffic, and inquiries over time.


### When Does It Make Sense to Get SEO Help?


Consider outside help when you encounter:


- Important pages that aren’t being crawled or indexed correctly
- Sitewide technical or performance problems
- Navigation or site structure that needs significant changes
- Many weak or overlapping pages that need a larger content plan
- Ongoing SEO strategies, including SEO and AEO work
- A priority list you don’t have time to execute consistently.
